title: Quantitation of nutrient metabolism in brain tumor patients using advanced 13C isotopomer technology
text:
More than 200,000 patients every year are affected by malignant brain tumors and these tumors
show very high proliferation with increased energy demand for their growth. The goal of this proposal
is to identify the key energy sources for brain tumor growth in patients through a translational
molecular imaging approach that uses non-radioactive 13C-enriched nutrients and NMR
Spectroscopy. Expected outcome of this study will generate key information to develop new targeted
therapy.

title: Development of iPSCs for comparative genomics in primates
text:
We propose to continue to develop, and freely share with the community, panels of matched induced pluripotent
stem cell (iPSCs) and established organoids, from humans and chimpanzees as a new transformative model system
for comparative functional genomic studies in primates.

title: Vevo F2 Imaging System
text:
Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death among adults in the US, and a leading cause of
death worldwide. The Molecular Cardiology Research Institute (MCRI) of Tufts Medical Center focuses on
understanding the scientific underpinnings of cardiovascular disease with the goal of informing new therapies
and diagnostic approaches. This application proposes to receive support to acquire the FUJIFILM Vevo F2
ultrasound system, the preeminent experimental cardiovascular imaging system in the world. Acquisition of the
Vevo F2 would provide our Institute with a single system to image our multi-species array of experimental models.
Thus, this device would have an enormous impact on MCRI studies, and to the advancement of cardiovascular
medicine.

title: Transcript RNA-mediated mechanisms in end-joining repair of DNA double-strand breaks
text:
Double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA are critical lesions that threaten genome stability and, if not properly
repaired, can lead to cancer and other degenerative diseases. This project investigates how RNA transcripts,
through their sequence complementarity to broken DNA ends, facilitate DSB repair in chromosomal DNA via
non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) in both human
embryonic kidney (HEK293T) cells and normal immortalized diploid human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE-1)
cells. By uncovering novel RNA-mediated repair mechanisms, the findings of this project could lead to new
therapeutic strategies for genome instability disorders and improve the precision of genome editing
technologies, with far-reaching implications for treating genetic diseases and cancer.

title: Biomechanical Determinants of Hematopoietic Stem Cell Potential
text:
Outcomes following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for treatment of blood disorders and hematologic
malignancies are limited by the availability and quality of donor-matched sources of bone marrow, mobilized
peripheral blood, and cord blood. To date, efforts to expand hematopoietic stem cells in culture and develop
alternative sources of stem cells have resulted in relatively poor self-renewal, skewed lineage potential, or low
engraftment efficiencies. The goal of the current research is to leverage new knowledge supporting an executive
role for mitochondrial remodeling in acquisition of hematopoietic fate in the embryo to establish new methods for
engineering scalable sources of hematopoietic stem cells that possess long-term, multi-lineage engraftment
potential.

title: Uncovering the spatial lipid-gene relationships underlying type 1 diabetes using multimodal imaging
text:
We propose a multimodal approach to uncover the lipid heterogeneity of the type 1 diabetic pancreas. We will
map lipids, RNA transcripts, and key protein markers using an established pipeline that integrates imaging mass
spectrometry, liquid chromatography mass spectrometry, spatial transcriptomics, and multiplexed
immunofluorescence. Datasets will be computationally integrated with existing NIH-supported pancreas datasets
within PanKbase and ingested into this repository to benefit the diabetes research community.

title: Overcoming Lenacapavir Resistance: Next-Generation Ultra-Potent HIV-1 Capsid Inhibitors
text:
Long-acting antiviral therapies have recently been breakthroughs in HIV treatment, yet their success is
threatened by a low barrier to drug resistance. Using the knowledge we have gained from more than 10 years
of experience in studying HIV CA-targeting antivirals, we have been able to design new compounds and
demonstrated that are exceptionally potent against both wild-type and drug-resistant strains of HIV. Further
development of such compounds could result in new treatment strategies, including combinations that could
transform HIV treatment and prevention.

title: Neuroimaging Multi-Omics Fingerprints for Subtyping and Uncertainty-Aware Prediction of Alzheimer's Disease
text:
Alzheimer's disease is a major health challenge, and the factors underlying its diverse progression remain poorly
understood. This project develops computational methods that combine brain imaging and multi-omics data to
identify distinctive Alzheimer's subtypes and provide probabilistic forecasts of disease progression. The results
will advance early detection and precision medicine while providing undergraduate students with interdisciplinary
research experience in neuroscience and artiﬁcial intelligence.

title: Elucidating the representational geometries underlying deductive reasoning, generalization, and flexible response generation.
text:
Psychiatric disorders can disrupt many of the cognitive processes through which we are able to flexibly adjust
our behavior to fit our current circumstances. For example, switching between different sets of rules to guide our
behavior from one moment to the next; drawing on past experiences to quickly fit into new situations; or more
subtly modifying certain aspects of our behavior while keeping others the same are all aspects of cognitive
flexibility that are impacted in mental illness, but the specific brain activity patterns that underlie these capacities
are not well described. This grant seeks to better understand how these behaviors are supported by specific
patterns of activity across a circuit spanning the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and motor output pathways.

title: PET/CT Imaging of Venous Thromboembolism in Pediatric, Adolescent, and Young Adult Oncology
text:
Venous thromboembolism (VTE) is an increasingly prevalent problem for pediatric, adolescent, and young adult
(AYA) cancer patients, which can be partially attributed to off-target effects of chemotherapy treatments that
damage the vascular endothelium and create a pro-inflammatory environment. PET/CT imaging with the
radionuclide 18F-FDG is standard of care for monitoring treatment responses in many cancers, but could provide
additional insight into chemotherapy-induced venous toxicity and risk for VTE events by allowing for quantitative
assessment of serial changes in venous inflammation. In this project, we will validate 18F-FDG PET/CT imaging
as a non-invasive approach for evaluating chemotherapy-induced venous toxicity and risk for VTE events,
thereby laying the foundation for the use of image-derived measures of venous inflammation to enhance
personalized plans for thromboprophylaxis and promote improved quality of life for pediatric and AYA cancer
patients.

title: Data and Omics Sciences Core
text: DATAOMICS CORE PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT The overarching role of the Data and Omics Sciences Core (DATAOmics) is to support and bolster collaborative cancer research in the Addressing Cancer Health Drivers and Infection-Driven Malignancies Program (ACTION). The overall goal of DATAOmics is to enhance the quality, efficiency, and impact of ACTION’s research projects through the provision of high-quality and timely data science and omics analysis, collaboration, and consulting at all stages of research – i.e., concept development, study design, data gathering and management, database design and use, statistical analysis, and reporting. Since 2004, previous versions of DATAOmics have provided consulting and computational support in study design and statistical analysis for projects within the research partnership and for UPRCCC, including trainees. We propose to continue these relationships. To support the development of investigators and trainees, we will provide capacitybuilding in study design, statistical and bioinformatics methods, data management, and reproducibility through educational activities in collaboration with the Research Education Core. As we conduct these activities, we will mentor partnership researchers in study design and in robust, reproducible data science to position our trainees at the leading edge of cancer science. Our experienced, collaborative team will achieve our aims of supporting and elevating the data science sophistication and capacity within ACTION, increasing publications in high-impact journals and applications for external research funding. Successful completion of our aims will be a vital component of ACTION’s goals to improve the health of Texans and Puerto Ricans and ultimately achieve NCI designation for UPRCCC. In sum, these activities are organized into the following three aims.

title: Neural Control of Cardiovascular Physiology via A Heart-to-Brain Pathway
text:
This project will investigate how vagal sensory neurons in the heart detect sensory stimuli in
blood circulation during acute hemorrhage and activate brain circuits that regulate
cardiovascular reflexes. By combining genetic, physiological, and imaging approaches, I aim to
identify distinct neural pathways that coordinate adaptive responses to circulatory stress.
Understanding these mechanisms can improve interventions for conditions such as
hemorrhagic shock, cardiovascular collapse, and cardiac injury.

title: Mechanical regulation of intestine stem cell-mediated tissue homeostasis in Drosophila
text:
In addition to its nutrient-absorption functions, gut epithelium is the site in which neural,
immune, microbial and dietary factors interact. These multi-system interactions critically
regulate whole-body physiology ranging from metabolism, immunity to cognition. At the
foundation of these interactions are the healthy and balanced number of gut epithelial
cells. As the largest exposed surfaces of the body, billions of cells are shed from the
human gut epithelium every day. These lost cells are constantly replaced by intestine
stem cells. Activity of intestine stem cell has to be precisely controlled or it may cause
tumorigenesis. Currently, 200,000 new cases of gastrointestinal tract cancers are
reported each year. Therefore, deciphering the mechanisms that regulate intestine stem
cell behavior and gut homeostasis is important for understanding how gut homeostasis is
maintained in normal conditions but altered in diseases.

title: Hepatic Nicotinamide N-Methyltransferase (NNMT) as a Pathogenetic Mechanism and Therapeutic Target for Alcoholic Liver Disease
text:
Liver damage induced by chronic alcohol drinking (alcoholic liver disease, ALD) remains an important health
problem in the United States and ranks among the major causes of morbidity and mortality in the world, and
affects millions of patients worldwide each year, with no accepted therapy available to halt or reverse this
process in humans. The recent preliminary studies in our laboratory demonstrated that chronic alcohol
exposure is associated with increased expression of nicotinamide N-methyltransferase (NNMT) in the liver.
Our further investigations suggest that NNMT inhibition confers protection against alcohol-induced fatty liver
development, suggesting that NNMT plays a pathological role in the development of ALD and represent an
ideal therapeutic target for the clinical intervention. In this proposal, we will utilize state of the art approaches
to test our hypotheses using both cell culture and animal models.

title: Tissue Culture and Molecular core
text: (Tissue Culture/Molecular) Continuing funds are requested by 18 vision scientists (holding 20 eligible NEI R01 grants) and their personnel to support three resource cores and an administrative core in the merged Department of Ophthalmology, Visual and Anatomical Sciences (former Ophthalmology and Anatomy/Cell Biology (two) Departments). The Tissue Culture/Molecular (TC/M) core will be directed by Dr. Jena Steinle, an R01-funded investigator with significant expertise in tissue culture and molecular biology techniques. Together with the PI, and a research assistant, the environment and capability to conduct vision research at Wayne State University and affiliated institutions will be enhanced through prioritization of the work of NEI R01 funded investigators, their staff and students (graduate and fellows) in numerous aspects of both tissue culture and molecular biology. The TC/M core will provide vision scientists (priority for NEI R01 funded) with facilities and technical assistance that will assure quality and cost effectiveness of the work performed. This core will maintain and propagate ocular and other cell types, as well as provide investigators with genotyping, reverse transcription- polymerase chain reaction (RT) and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (q)-PCR, gene silencing-siRNA, shRNA, CRISPR/Cas9, nested PCR and adherence assays. It will also provide for consultation on recombinant (r) AAV virus vector use (at no cost) and advice to the PI, students or staff for in vitro functional assessments. Overall, the TC/M core will assist NEI R01-funded investigators and their staff/students in studies that require the use of tissue culture and molecular biology techniques; foster collaboration between vision scientists using tissue culture and molecular biological techniques; and bring new investigators into vision research by providing assistance in tissue culture and molecular techniques that will expand their research focus.

title: Deciphering the role of MLL-partial tandem duplication in AML through integrated genomic and proteomic approaches
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because understanding the mechanism by which MLLPTD
drives disease progression in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is critical for guiding the development of new ther-
apeutic strategies for patients. This work aligns with the NIH’s mission to advance fundamental knowledge and
reduce the burden of human disease.

title: Gene therapy for disorders of the extracellular matrix
text:
Gould syndrome – caused by mutations in type IV collagen alpha 1 (COL4A1) and alpha 2 (COL4A2) – is a
multisystem disorder critically involving the cerebral vasculature and for which there are no interventions. The
mechanisms by which mutations lead to disease are complex and poorly understood representing a barrier to
development of mechanism-based interventions. However, because it is a devastating, dominant disorder, Gould
syndrome is an ideal candidate for correction via genome editing technologies. This study will provide the pre-
clinical data needed to develop personalized treatments for patients with Gould syndrome and other extracellular
matrix disorders.

title: Multiplexed detection of cell-free M. Tuberculosis DNA and its drug-resistant variants in blood
text:
Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading cause of death from infectious disease worldwide, but can be challenging to
diagnose due to the poor performance of current diagnostic tests that require sputum or tissue biopsies that can
be difficult to obtain in certain patient populations, including young children, and this situation has worsened due
the reallocation of healthcare resources during the COVID-19 pandemic. We thus propose to employ a novel
CRISPR-based paper strip point-of-care assay to detect and quantify Mycobacterium tuberculosis-derived cell-
free DNA (Mtb-cfDNA) in blood to simplify sample collection for the diagnosis and treatment evaluation of drug-
sensitive and -resistent TB cases. Based on our preliminary studies, we are confident that this assay will improve
TB diagnosis in all patient populations, including the diagnosis of early disease in young children, and allow
consistent evaluation of Mtb-cfDNA changes that should reflect the systemic effects of anti-TB treatment, both
of which are required to improve TB control efforts in resource-limited areas with high endemic TB levels.

title: Structure, function, and antigenicity of emerging henipavirus surface glycoproteins
text:
Henipaviruses that can spread from animal to human and between humans have caused repeated outbreaks
with high case fatality rates. To counteract the growing threat posed by the expanding henipavirus members, we
will structurally and functionally characterize their surface glycoproteins G and F and to identify sites of
vulnerability using protective antibodies. The result of this study will pave the way for future development of
effective vaccine and therapeutics against these viruses.

title: Fluorescence-based detection of inflammation and necrosis to inform surgical decision-making and enhance outcomes
text: The proposed project investigates fluorescence image-guided surgery to allow precise identification of necrotic tissue both preoperatively and intraoperatively in burn patients. Furthermore, it uses a multi-model approach to elucidate the localization of indocyanine green inflammation and necrosis to determine how this novel use of a well-known fluorescence marker can be optimized to aid in surgical decision making. This proposal will provide the necessary data to support the design of a larger clinical trial to study the feasibility and efficacy of this technology to improve the precision of necrosis detection and removal and improve wound healing outcomes.
